title: Thousands of Minnesotans May Be Canadian Citizens Without Knowing It
excerpt: A change to Canada's Citizenship Act that took effect in December 2025 removed the first-generation limit — and with it, the cap on how far back claims can run.
body:
• Bill C-3, which amended Canada's Citizenship Act, took effect on December 15, 2025, removing the first-generation limit on citizenship by descent.
  • Census data shows more than 6,000 Minnesotans reporting Canadian ancestry and more than 41,000 reporting French Canadian ancestry — roughly 47,000 ancestry responses with a potential claim to a Canadian citizenship certificate.
  • Minnesotans with an unbroken line of descent from even one Canadian ancestor may already be dual Canadian-American citizens, even if no one in the family has lived in Canada for generations.
  • How to claim it: file a proof-of-citizenship application with the Canadian government. An approved certificate unlocks a Canadian passport, the right to live and work in Canada, and youth-mobility access to 35-plus countries for those under 30 (35 in some cases) — and it does not, on its own, create Canadian tax obligations.

A border state's hidden dual citizens

Ask Americans to name the most Canadian corner of the United States, and most will point to New England. But just north of St. Paul, in Ramsey County, Minnesota, sits a city literally called Little Canada — its water tower spells out the name, its flag carries a maple leaf. It is one of many reminders of how tightly Minnesota is tied to its northern neighbour: the state shares a border with Ontario and Manitoba, and French Canadian names are scattered across its map.

https://x.com/canadavisa_com/status/2107788453689913522

Thanks to a Canadian law that took effect in December 2025, those ties may mean far more than shared hockey loyalties and politeness. Tens of thousands of Minnesota residents may now be dual Canadian-American citizens through their ancestry — and most have no idea.

What changed

Bill C-3, which amended Canada's Citizenship Act, came into force on December 15, 2025. It removed the first-generation limit — the rule that had stopped Canadian citizens born abroad from passing citizenship to children who were also born abroad. With that cap gone, a claim can run down an entire family line from a single Canadian-born ancestor, regardless of how many generations have passed since anyone lived in Canada.

The U.S. Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey five-year estimates put the scale in perspective: more than 6,000 Minnesotans report Canadian ancestry and more than 41,000 report French Canadian ancestry. Canada's citizenship rules do not distinguish between the two — a French Canadian ancestor counts the same as any other. Combined, that is roughly 47,000 ancestry responses with a potential claim. And the true number is likely higher: ancestry is self-reported, families lose track of where a great-grandparent was born, and a single qualifying ancestor can carry a claim down an entire family line.

The French Canadian thread

The numbers are no accident. The French Canadian settlement that became Little Canada traces to Benjamin Gervais, a French Canadian voyageur and farmer who moved north of St. Paul in 1844 and founded a French-speaking farming community. By 1895, an estimated 70,000 French Canadian immigrants lived in Minnesota and its neighbouring states — a community large enough to sustain its own French-language press. Minnesota's state motto, L'Étoile du Nord — French for 'The Star of the North' — honours the French Canadian explorers and settlers who arrived before statehood.

What eligibility actually requires

A Canadian ancestor alone does not guarantee a certificate. Each generational link between the applicant and that ancestor must be backed by supporting documents from an original source authority — birth certificates, marriage records, and the like. But the bar is documentation, not residence: as CIC News notes, eligible Minnesotans need only apply to formally claim their status through a proof-of-citizenship application. Approved applicants receive a Canadian citizenship certificate, which confirms their status and opens the door to a Canadian passport.

The upside is concrete. U.S.-Canadian dual citizens can enter, live, and work in Canada. Those under 30 — or 35 in some cases — can use Canada's youth mobility arrangements to live and work in more than 35 countries, most of them in Europe. And there is little downside: a citizenship certificate does not, on its own, create Canadian tax obligations, since Canadian income tax generally depends on where a person lives and where their income comes from.

Diaspora angle

The C-3 change reaches well beyond Minnesota. Indian-Canadian families who moved to the United States are among the most directly affected: U.S.-born children of Canadian citizens, once cut off by the first-generation limit, may now be Canadian citizens already. For a diaspora that straddles both countries — students, tech workers, and families split between Toronto and Seattle — a dormant claim can mean an extra passport, a second labour market, and European mobility options for the next generation.

What's next

Claims will rise or fall on paperwork: families who dig into their genealogy and assemble the documents stand to gain the most. If your family tree includes a relative who came down from Quebec or Manitoba — or one who farmed near Little Canada — it may be worth a closer look.
